report:
Your “no” is essentially right for ordinary chronic subjective tinnitus: ginkgo has **no proven symptom-relieving benefit**, and major guidance advises against it. The evidence is not absolutely zero—some small or industry-linked trials report improvements—but higher-quality syntheses find effects inconsistent, biased, or no better than placebo.

A Cochrane summary of trials where tinnitus was the primary complaint found “no evidence that Ginkgo biloba is effective,” with few good-quality studies despite 1,543 participants: https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus. A later Cochrane/PubMed abstract is more cautious, saying benefits and harms versus placebo are uncertain and evidence certainty is low to very low—still not a basis to recommend it: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36383762/. The AAO-HNS tinnitus guideline is stronger clinically: clinicians “should NOT recommend ginkgo biloba” or other dietary supplements for tinnitus: https://www.entnet.org/resource/aao-hnsf-cpg-tinnitus-press-release-fact-sheet/. An earlier systematic review likewise found no convincing statistical proof of efficacy across randomized placebo-controlled trials: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/.

Practical caveat: tinnitus can signal treatable or urgent problems. Seek prompt care for pulsatile tinnitus, one-sided tinnitus, sudden hearing loss, neurologic symptoms, or severe distress. Also note ginkgo can increase bleeding risk and interact with anticoagulants/antiplatelets, so “natural” does not mean risk-free.
